title: Knowledge Check 3: Lessons 11-15
description: Questions pooled from Lessons 11-15 of the hermes-consultant-advanced series. Score 80% or higher to progress toward the practice exam.

questions.question: Why is the unit of analysis for portfolio management the account rather than a single engagement?
options: Because accounts are billed monthly while engagements are billed on milestones.
Because the levers cross engagement boundaries, so the relationship needs an owner accountable beyond the work in flight.
Because clients insist on one point of contact for commercial questions.
Because engagement-level data is not available in the delivery system.
questions.explanation: The expansion, renewal, and churn levers act on the whole relationship, so the unit of analysis is the account rather than one engagement.

questions.question: What is the strategic test for whether an expansion genuinely improves the portfolio?
options: Reuse: whether the next engagement can lean on captured skills and method, so marginal cost falls.
Whether the account will pay a higher rate for the second engagement than the first.
Whether the expansion keeps the delivery team at full utilization.
Whether the expansion is larger in revenue than the engagement it follows.
questions.explanation: An expansion compounds only when it reuses existing capability, lowering marginal cost instead of pulling the team into a new domain.

questions.question: An account buys the lowest-margin work and drains senior capability from the practice. How should a principal treat it?
options: Renew it but staff it with junior operators to protect the margin.
Keep it, since all revenue is good and churn is always the enemy.
Convert it to an hourly model so the attention cost becomes visible.
Treat it as a candidate for intentional churn, freeing capability for accounts that compound.
questions.explanation: An account that consumes more capability than it returns is worth winding down deliberately, so the freed capability can fund accounts that compound.

questions.question: A buyer challenges the price and says other vendors quoted less. What is the sound response?
options: Offer a discount to keep the deal alive, since a lost deal costs more than a thinner margin.
Explain that the other vendors are not credible and ask the buyer to disregard them.
Reduce the scope silently to fit the lower price without telling the buyer.
Return to the value: restate what changes, what it is worth, and what it costs the buyer not to act.
questions.explanation: A price challenge usually means the buyer does not yet see the value; discounting teaches that the price was arbitrary, while returning to value answers the real question.

questions.question: How do the estimate and the price relate to each other?
options: The price is the estimate plus a standard markup the practice chooses.
The estimate is internal effort against the practice's method, while the price is the value the market will bear.
The estimate should equal the price so the delivery team is protected.
The price is the estimate discounted by whatever the buyer's budget allows.
questions.explanation: The estimate answers an internal effort question, while the price is a separate judgment about what the work is worth to the buyer.

questions.question: Where is most scope creep actually prevented?
options: In scoping and the proposal, by naming every deliverable, assumption, and exclusion.
In change control, once the engagement is underway and requests arrive.
In the contract, by reserving the right to re-price new requests.
In delivery, by absorbing small requests so the client stays happy.
questions.explanation: A vague boundary at scoping is what invites later creep, so the proposal is where the tight scope and its exclusions are set.

questions.question: When should a practice write down a reference architecture?
options: As soon as it decides to offer a class of work, so the first engagement can follow it.
After the second or third time it has done that kind of work, once the shape has repeated.
Only after a client asks for a formal methodology document.
Whenever a competitor publishes an equivalent pattern for the same problem.
questions.explanation: A pattern is only trustworthy once it has been earned by repetition, so a premature reference architecture is confident and wrong.

questions.question: Which three properties separate compounding internal tooling from a one-off expense?
options: It is fast, cheap, and fully automated.
It is documented, approved, and version controlled.
It is reused, improves with use, and has a named owner.
It is generic, portable, and independent of any single client.
questions.explanation: Tooling compounds only when it is reused, improves with each use, and has a named owner to keep it current.

questions.question: What is the failure mode of accumulated machinery that is never reviewed?
options: It outlives its accuracy, so a stale pattern is trusted and followed with confidence.
It grows faster than the practice can document it.
It becomes too specific to the clients it was built for.
It discourages the team from solving new problems from first principles.
questions.explanation: A stale pattern is worse than no pattern because it is trusted, so each asset needs an owner and a review cadence.

questions.question: What is the core reason for forming a legal entity rather than contracting as an individual?
options: To reduce the tax the practice pays on consulting income.
To separate the practice's obligations from the person's, so a liability does not reach personal assets.
To make invoicing simpler for enterprise clients.
To allow the practice to hire contractors without a written agreement.
questions.explanation: An entity separates the practice's obligations from the person's, so a claim against the company does not reach personal assets.

questions.question: Why is separating the practice's money from the founder's personal money the first financial act?
options: Because it is required before the practice can file a tax return.
Because mixing the two makes the founder personally liable for business debts.
Because a practice whose revenue and cost land in one set of books can compute what it costs to deliver, so it can price.
Because clients will not contract with a practice that pays personal expenses.
questions.explanation: Separate books are what make revenue and cost comparable, which is the only way to know what it costs to deliver and how to price.

questions.question: What does the practice require of the ownership of its functions?
options: Every function has a named owner, so when a person leaves their functions are already named and can be reassigned.
The principal should own every function until the practice can afford a dedicated operator.
Ownership can stay implicit as long as the team is small and communicates well.
Only the reference architectures and internal tooling need named owners.
questions.explanation: Named ownership means a departure surfaces no hidden dependency, since each function is already assigned to someone.

questions.question: What is the difference between quality control and quality assurance?
options: Control applies to software deliverables and assurance applies to client relationships.
Control inspects an output and decides whether it passes, while assurance shapes the process so defects do not arise.
Control is documented and assurance is informal.
Control is done by the author and assurance by an external auditor.
questions.explanation: Control is inspection at the point of delivery, while assurance designs the process so the defect is never created, which is cheaper.

questions.question: What is the hard requirement for a gate in a quality system?
options: That it happens at the point of delivery so nothing ships unreviewed.
That it is recorded in the quality system before the work advances.
That it has a named reviewer and a written checklist of criteria.
Separation: the author of the work does not pass their own work.
questions.explanation: A gate only works if the person who produced the work is not the one who passes it, since authors miss their own mistakes.

questions.question: A practice is deciding whether to pursue a certification. What is the sound approach?
options: Pursue every major certification so the practice can answer any procurement question.
Skip certification entirely and rely on internal records as evidence.
Build the system because it improves the work, then certify only when a real buyer gates on it.
Buy the certificate first, then let the system catch up.
questions.explanation: Certification is worth buying only where a buyer actually requires it; the system itself should be built to improve the work, not to win a badge.
